probe/ask: Halfway up a model, a word's residual stream is hundreds of numbers. Does it know whether the word is a noun? Reading the numbers by eye will not tell you.
probe/points: Collect the stream at that layer, h, for many words, and pretend it holds just two numbers: each word is a point.
probe/labels: Each word comes with its right answer, noun or not, called its label, y. Color the points by label.
probe/line: Train a linear classifier on these points, as before: weights, w, turn its line, and a bias, b, slides it, until it splits the colors as well as it can.
probe/score: Its score, w dot h plus b, is positive on the noun side. If the line splits the colors well, the stream holds the answer where a linear classifier can read it.
probe/frozen: Only w and b are trained; the model stays frozen. That is why this is called a probe: an instrument that measures a system without changing it, like a thermometer.
probe/history: Guillaume Alain and Yoshua Bengio named these linear classifiers probes in 2016, and fit one on every layer of trained image networks.
score/wb: Say training gave w as one and two, and b as minus one.
score/yes: Take a word at the point one, one. Its score is one, plus two, minus one: two. Positive, so the probe says noun.
score/no: Another word sits at zero and minus one. Its score is zero, minus two, minus one: minus three. Negative: not a noun.
score/dir: Exactly zero sits on the line. And w is a direction: the probe weighs every number in the stream, not just one.
classes/three: A probe can read out more than yes or no: say, a sentence's tense, past, present or future. Each point now has one of three labels.
classes/regions: Each class gets its own weights and bias, as in any linear classifier, and the highest score wins: three regions with straight borders.
classes/h: A new word's stream, h, is one and two. It lands in the present region.
classes/W: Stack the weight rows into a matrix, W, and the biases into b: one row and one bias per class.
classes/row: Row zero, w zero, is past's. Dot it with h and add its bias: two times one, plus zero times two, minus one, is one.
classes/all: Present's row gives two, and future's minus two. Two is the highest, so the probe says present: the region h landed in.
test/held: Then test the probe on held-out words: words kept aside, never trained on. A score above zero predicts noun.
test/count: It matches their labels on six of eight: an accuracy of zero point seven five, where a coin flip gets a half.
meaning/there: High accuracy shows the answer is in the stream, readable by one linear map: a weighted sum, like the probe's score.
meaning/use: It does not show that the model uses it. Being there is not being used: testing use takes changing the stream and watching the model.
meaning/random: The probe must also stay simple. In 2019, John Hewitt and Percy Liang gave each word a random label, one no stream could know. An MLP probe still got about ninety three percent right, by memorizing.
meaning/linear: A linear probe got only about seventy one, though both got about ninety seven on the real labels. A line can barely memorize, so its success describes the stream. If only a big probe succeeds, the big probe may be doing the work.
